stem: A sponsor states the goal as reducing fraud-dispute resolution time without raising the false-approval rate, and names no system or pattern. A regulator requires each decision to be auditable within five business days. What should the architect do next?

opts.t: Run a model benchmark on historical dispute data to ground the target in evidence.
Proceed to bounding the requirement: set the target time, the false-approval ceiling, how each is measured, and the audited population.
Assess whether the sponsor's named detection pattern fits the stated goal before scoping further.
Escalate to the sponsor's leadership that a five-day audit window makes this requirement unworkable.

whyRight: The sponsor has already stated the business outcome and the regulator's constraint, so discovery's precondition is met; no pattern was named to redirect. What remains is turning the goal into a bounded target: a number, a measurement method, and the audited population.

whyWrong.A: Benchmarking now produces an accuracy number before any target or error cost exists to judge it against — evidence before there is anything to interpret it for.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the sponsor named no system or pattern, so there is nothing to assess for fit; this answers a situation that has not occurred.
whyWrong.D: Treats the regulator's audit window as an obstacle to escalate rather than as a design input the bounded requirement must account for.

stem: A sponsor is planning next quarter's legal-review staffing using the contract-extraction model's own 92% accuracy figure. Performance is uniform across contract types, but low-confidence extractions still route to human reviewers before any output ships. What should the architect supply instead?

opts.t: The full monitoring dashboard, so the sponsor can select whichever metrics matter to the staffing decision.
The end-to-end outcome, including the human-review step, since the sponsor is accountable for the whole process, not the model alone.
Accuracy broken out by contract type, with the measurement method and evaluation set stated.
The model's accuracy figure alone, with the measurement method and evaluation set stated.

whyRight: The sponsor is planning a staffing decision, which is accountable for the whole delivered process, not the model component; the 92% figure omits the human-review step that still touches every low-confidence case, so the end-to-end outcome is what the decision actually needs.

whyWrong.A: Handing over the full dashboard is thorough-looking but transfers the interpretation work to a sponsor without the context to weigh model metrics against a staffing number.
whyWrong.C: The stem states performance is uniform across contract types, so segmentation adds nothing here; the gap is the missing human-review step, not hidden variance.
whyWrong.D: A correctly qualified model figure is still the wrong axis when human review sits between the model and every shipped output the sponsor is staffing against.

t1Clause: low-confidence extractions still route to human reviewers before any output ships
lessonKey: end human included outcome steps supply

stem: A signed contract already commits the provider to 99% classification accuracy, measured monthly, across all document types, and the client's legal team refuses to reopen the contract language before go-live. What should the architect do next?

opts.t: Build the system and its monitoring to meet the 99% figure as contracted, and manage the risk internally.
Go back to legal and propose renegotiating the SLA into a segmented commitment with named exclusions.
Tell the client's leadership the 99% commitment cannot be met and should be dropped from the contract.
Commit voluntarily to a higher accuracy figure to build a safety margin against the contracted number.

whyRight: The signed contract, not the architect's preferred framing, is the binding requirement here, and legal has already closed the door on reopening it before go-live. The engagement's task is to design and monitor toward the stated figure and manage the input-mix risk internally.

whyWrong.B: Renegotiating into a more defensible, segmented SLA is the right move when the commitment is still open — legal has already stated it is not, for this engagement.
whyWrong.C: Declaring the commitment unmeetable and asking to drop it abandons a signed obligation instead of designing and monitoring toward it.
whyWrong.D: Volunteering a stricter figure adds cost and risk to an already-fixed commitment without addressing the actual constraint: the client's unmanaged input mix.

t1Clause: the client's legal team refuses to reopen the contract language before go-live
lessonKey: 99 build contracted figure internally manage meet monitoring risk system

stem: A receiving team already holds the interface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes, and gating tests for a delivered system. Their manager separately requests a plain-language onboarding overview to ramp new engineers within the sprint. How should the architect respond?

opts.t: Provide the overview as a supplement; it orients new readers but does not replace the contracts, rationale, or gating tests.
Replace the interface contracts and gating tests with the new overview, since it covers the same ground more accessibly.
Decline the request, since the existing implementation guidance is already the complete artifact the team needs.
Supply the failure-mode list and gating tests, since the receiving team does not yet have that guidance.

whyRight: The team already holds the gating artifacts, so the overview request is additive, not a gap to fill. An onboarding overview orients a new reader; it is a supplement to the contracts, rationale, and tests, and does not gate any future change on its own.

whyWrong.B: A narrative overview reads as complete and reassuring, but it gates no change; substituting it for the contracts and tests removes the only artifact that does.
whyWrong.C: Declining a reasonable onboarding request treats it as an intrusion rather than a legitimate supplement that sits alongside guidance already delivered.
whyWrong.D: The stem already states the team holds the failure-mode list and gating tests, so supplying them again answers a gap that does not exist here.

t1Clause: already holds the interface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes, and gating tests

stem: A delivered system transfers to the client's internal team with repository access, documentation, and completed training; no post-launch issues have appeared. The contract requires independent quality detection once vendor support ends in 60 days. Select two items the handover must still add.

opts.t: Assign accountability to the receiving team as a whole, rather than to one named person.
A named owner, with a deputy, accountable for the system once vendor support ends.
The evaluation suite and its acceptance thresholds, plus the cadence for re-running them.
Investigate input-distribution shift and re-run the evaluation suite now, the standard response to silent degradation.

whyRight: Repository access, documentation, and training make the system runnable but not detectable: nothing in that bundle shows the receiving team whether it is still working once the vendor is gone. A named owner and an evaluation suite with thresholds and cadence are the missing pieces that make degradation visible.

whyWrong.A: A team-wide assignment is a distributed owner, which the section treats as no owner; accountability for a re-check routine needs one named person and a deputy.
whyWrong.D: Re-running the suite in response to a shift is the correct move once complaints or drift actually appear; none have, so this answers a symptom that has not occurred.

stem: A compliance officer requires that every flagged insurance claim receive sign-off from two independent human reviewers, citing a binding audit standard. An automated cross-check model reaches equivalent measured accuracy at far lower review cost. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Replace the second human reviewer with the automated cross-check model, since measured accuracy is equivalent at lower cost.
Design a three-layer automated consensus and audit-trail system that exceeds the stated dual sign-off requirement for added assurance.
Implement the two-reviewer sign-off exactly as stated for every flagged claim, since the named mechanism is itself the audit-mandated requirement.
Apply two-reviewer sign-off only to the highest-risk claims and route the rest through the automated cross-check to cut load.

whyRight: The dual sign-off is the audit standard's own mechanism, not the architect's proxy for an accuracy target — it stays in place regardless of what an equivalent-accuracy substitute measures, because the requirement being satisfied is the named control itself, not a general error rate.

whyWrong.A: Equivalent measured accuracy does not satisfy a mandated control; the requirement is the two-reviewer mechanism itself, so substituting automation drops the compliance obligation it exists to meet.
whyWrong.B: A more elaborate consensus system is not what the audit standard asks for; exceeding the stated mechanism is out of scope, however defensible it looks on engineering grounds.
whyWrong.D: Partial application leaves flagged claims outside the highest-risk segment without the sign-off the standard requires on every flagged claim, not just the riskiest subset.

lessonKey: audit claim every exactly flagged implement itself mandated mechanism named off requirement reviewer sign since stated two

stem: A stakeholder assumes 10% of expense-report categorizations still needing human review reflects an accuracy or compliance limit. No regulator or sign-off rule governs the segment; it was simply deprioritized during the build. What should the architect say?

opts.t: Name the specific decisions in that 10% carrying accountability or attestation requirements, and the risk of automating each.
Commit to removing the review immediately, since the segment carries low risk and needs no further justification.
Decline to estimate the cost of closing the gap, since pricing engineering work is outside the architect's remit.
Say the segment is low-risk and simply unbuilt, not a principled limit, and price what closing the gap would cost.

whyRight: Not every human step is a regulatory or accountability limit; where no attestation rule governs the segment, the honest answer names it as an unbuilt, low-risk gap and prices the investment needed to close it, rather than manufacturing a principled justification.

whyWrong.A: The stem states no regulator or sign-off rule governs this segment, so framing it as an accountability limit contradicts the facts already given.
whyWrong.B: Low risk justifies removing the human step but does not excuse skipping the honest statement and the cost of closing the gap.
whyWrong.C: Pricing an automation gap is exactly the input the stakeholder needs to decide whether closing it is worth funding.

t1Clause: No regulator or sign-off rule governs this segment

stem: A logistics client on a high-volume, shared provider-hosted classification endpoint insists the contract state a flat two-second maximum response time with no exceptions. Which latency commitment should the architect propose?

opts.t: Commit to an average response time across all requests instead of a maximum figure.
Commit a latency percentile, such as the 95th, since tail latency on a shared endpoint is not fully controllable.
Decline any contractual latency commitment, since a shared endpoint's response time cannot be guaranteed.
Commit to the flat two-second maximum exactly as requested, since latency is a provider-controlled metric.

whyRight: Latency and availability are provider-controlled and can be committed, but a shared endpoint's tail behaviour is not fully within the provider's control; a percentile commitment states what is actually keepable, where a flat maximum promises more than the architecture can guarantee.

whyWrong.A: An average conceals the tail spikes that actually break an SLA on a shared endpoint, so it does not answer the client's stated maximum-latency concern.
whyWrong.C: Declining any commitment leaves the client unable to plan against a service they are paying for, dropping a commitment that a percentile could have kept.
whyWrong.D: The stem already states the endpoint is shared; treating latency as fully provider-controlled on a multi-tenant service is ruled out by that fact.

stem: A receiving team gets a document listing every threshold in a high-volume triage system, with no explanation of why each was set. An engineer later lowers the confidence threshold to cut review volume, undoing a cost-driven calibration. What was missing?

opts.t: A narrative overview explaining how the full triage pipeline reasons end to end.
A support channel where the original team answers questions about configuration changes after they ship.
The rationale behind each threshold, so its load-bearing role is visible before anyone changes it.
Regression tests confirming the pipeline still runs correctly after any configuration change ships.

whyRight: A configuration value without its reason looks arbitrary and inconvenient to the next engineer who tunes it; only the rationale makes visible that the threshold was calibrated against an asymmetric error cost, not a default worth adjusting for convenience.

whyWrong.A: A pipeline-level narrative describes behaviour in general terms; it does not flag that one specific threshold was load-bearing against a cost calibration.
whyWrong.B: A support channel depends on the original team staying reachable and reacts after a value has already been changed, not before.
whyWrong.D: Passing pipeline tests confirms the system still runs; it does not reveal that a specific threshold's value was chosen for a cost reason.

t1Clause: lowers the confidence threshold to cut review volume
